guidance: Do not use this tool as the sole basis for protective or emergency decisions. Follow current authoritative procedures and qualified guidance.
method: A non-self-supporting (leaning) ladder stands at the angle OSHA's construction rule describes: the foot is set back one quarter of the working length, the distance along the ladder from the foot to the top support (29 CFR 1926.1053(b)(5)(i)). With the set-back s and the working length L related by s = L/4, the support height is h = sqrt(L^2 - s^2) = L*sqrt(15)/4, so the page turns a height into L = h*4/sqrt(15) and s = h/sqrt(15). That pair always gives a lean of acos(0.25) = 75.5 degrees from horizontal, the same 75.5 degrees the standard names when it load-tests a portable ladder, and the page reports the angle as a check rather than as an input. Because a ladder used to reach an upper landing must stand at least 3 ft (0.9 m) above it (1926.1053(b)(1)), the rail length the page asks for is the working length plus that extension; a ladder between the working length and that rail length is reported as low rather than as wrong, with the standard's alternative of securing the top to a rigid support and providing a grasping device such as a grab rail. A ladder shorter than the working length is reported as short, because its rails never reach the support. Limits: a support height of 1 to 15 m and a rail length of 1 to 20 m, both convertible to feet at 0.3048 m per foot. The page warns above an 8 m climb, where a portable ladder is rarely the right access, and when more than 3 m of rail would stand above the landing. It is geometry only: it does not check the ladder's duty rating or condition, the ground, the tie-off, overhead lines or the footing, it does not apply to self-supporting stepladders (used fully open, top step never used as a step), and it does not decide whether a ladder is the right access for the job.
